slug: 2024-05-23-zhangxiaojun-前沿科技创业的痛-上市那天-我觉得对不起这12年
title: The pain of frontier tech startups: on the day of the IPO, I felt I had let down these 12 years
dek: Li Zhifei, founder of Mobvoi, says that at the moment of the bell-ringing he wasn't thinking of glory, but of ‘does today's result do justice to the 12 years of hardship I've endured—no, it doesn't.’ He sums up the fate of frontier tech startups as a block of ice that can melt at any time.
why: An AI founder who spent 12 years and just took his company public talks, unusually, about failure, depression and strategic misjudgment. High information density; the second half is worth more than the first.
who: Founders building large models or AI applications and agonizing over whether to go all in, and investors who want to see the real financial and strategic predicaments of AI companies.
skip: The IPO process details at the start, 2:00-8:36, can be fast-forwarded; low information density.

points.body: Li Zhifei proposes a ‘funnel model’: of 100 frontier technologies, only a tiny minority can be packaged from a technology into a product, form a business model, and reach a point where technology investment and commercial value match sustainably. Most technologies at that point in time cannot pass the funnel's test. But that doesn't mean the technology is useless—it may come back 10 years later, because the environment has changed, the technology has matured, demand has matured, or new demand has appeared, and the technology is taken out and put through the funnel again. He uses 2013's Google Glass as an example: at the time everyone literally saw the future, but the product quickly disappeared, and the entire AR and VR industry hasn't taken off in all these years; and now GPT-4o and Google have spawned glasses again, and you see the future again—it's back.

points.h: A vision without a path and rhythm plan is hooliganism
points.body: Li Zhifei says that telling a broad future is easy—in 2014 he was already saying every company would have an AI department, and a normal person wouldn't be too far off with that kind of judgment. What really matters is the judgment of path and rhythm: what to do first, what to do second. He gives two competitive scenarios: if a giant and a startup reach a consensus at the same time, and that consensus is wrong, the one that dies is definitely the startup, because it can't hold out; if the startup forms a cognition of the future half a year to a year before the giant, and has a relatively precise plan, then it has a certain probability of success—provided you can use that one-year time gap to build some kind of barrier, otherwise the startup will also die. He adds one more thing: even if the thing looks hopeless, as long as an investor is willing to give you a billion dollars, that can keep you alive.

points.h: The key to GPT-4o is unification plus end-to-end
points.body: Li Zhifei first states, ‘we don't know either, because he didn't write a paper, we're all guessing.’ He judges two core points: first, it is a unified single model, with all modalities in the same model; second, it is most likely based on the GPT architecture, using a language model as the foundation of cognition, then adding other perceptual modalities. He uses the analogy of teaching a monkey to cook and teaching a six-year-old child to cook—the child has built a cognitive model of the world, and you just describe in language how to cook; the monkey has no cognitive foundation. Why is it hard? You have to turn all modalities into tokens, like text. He mentions that his own model workshop's voiceover model was trained last April by adding voice on top of a language model, but the language model was too small, so it could only do voiceover, not Q&A. GPT-4o, on the one hand, can do speech generation and understanding, and on the other hand, its text cognitive ability hasn't declined, and it is even stronger than GPT-4 on MMLU.

points.h: There is voice generation, but no video generation
points.body: Li Zhifei noticed a detail: in GPT-4o's assistant model there is no video generation; whether Google or OpenAI, video generation is a separate model. He explains the reason is that Sora is not an autoregressive architecture, and is probably using DiT, a Diffusion architecture. He repeatedly emphasizes his belief: a unified model should be based on autoregression, putting understanding and generation together. He guesses that someone inside OpenAI must be working on this, but is not sure whether it is treated as the all-in direction—‘engineers have their own beliefs too; he feels autoregression is unhappy, he feels Diffusion is happier.’ He also gives the order-of-magnitude difference in token length: text is a few characters per second, voice is a few dozen tokens per second, video may be several hundred tokens per second, each is at least an order of magnitude increase, and token length directly determines the cost and speed of inference.

points.h: ByteDance's big price cut is inevitable; the API business model is unsustainable
points.body: Li Zhifei says ByteDance's big price cut ‘was inevitably going to be like this, and it will approach zero, infinitely close to zero.’ He tells a story: last September or October he was chatting with a large-model entrepreneur, who said that besides app revenue there was also API call revenue, and it could bring in quite a bit a year. He advised him on the spot to just shut it down, because ‘there's no reason you'd still be collecting that money next year.’ He says this form appeared in the AI 1.0 era—speech recognition, TTS calls; as soon as a giant entered, it became free, and there were even bids won for one yuan, it's just that the economy has been bad for the past few years and things quieted down. His judgment is: for the whole ecosystem and for users it's a good thing, it's great that giants are treating everyone to free use of large models; but for companies whose business model is API, it's not a good thing, you have to rethink what your business model is.

points.h: When making smartwatches, I didn't think about the ecological niche
points.body: Li Zhifei uses smartwatches to review his own strategic mistake: making smartwatches in 2015, from a strategic perspective, was perhaps just wrong. Why? Five years later, under full competition, there is no so-called ecological niche—phone manufacturers will all do it, and they can do it well as a side business, because the capabilities are completely common and overlapping with their phones. He says if he had had the method of the six elements of strategy at the time, he might have worked harder to think: choosing to make smartwatches, five years later when the giants are fully invested, how do I hold a position? Then he might have thought more about differentiation, and the execution path would have been different. He hypothesizes that if on day one back then he had gone all in on overseas, not done domestic, not done so much smart hardware, and used the limited time gap to build barriers, the state might have been more successful. The core is ‘it forces you to think.’

points.h: Zeng Ming said we are on a block of ice
points.body: At Hupan University, Li Zhifei raised as a case the question ‘in the AIGC era, three to five years from now, will we AI tools still have an ecological niche?’ Zeng Ming's answer was ‘definitely not,’ but ‘I think you've already done the best you can.’ Zeng Ming's metaphor is: today you are in a sea where the situation is particularly unclear, you are on a block of ice, at least you are not underwater, you are on the ice; but this ice may melt or flip at any time. So the posture you need is to run at low power, while very keenly observing whether there is solid ice around you; once there is solid ice, you must be ready, and you must still have the ability to jump onto it. Li Zhifei says that today all large-model companies probably have to adopt this posture—even if you've found a business model and have user volume, you are still on a block of ice.

points.h: The moment I saw the startup dying, I got depressed
points.body: Li Zhifei says that in 2019 he truly felt the company would die: there were only three or four hundred million RMB left in the account, but salaries alone cost over three hundred million a year, plus 400 million in inventory, over a thousand people, and 20 offline stores. He recalls that if Google hadn't given money it would also have died, maybe with only three or four months of money left in the account, it's just that he didn't look; in April 2014 Volkswagen gave 180 million USD, and if it had come four months later it might have died too. In 2020 the pandemic came, and instead of hitting bottom and rebounding, the bottom was that deep; he says ‘I think I got depressed,’ didn't want to talk to anyone, and it showed as the CEO no longer wanting to work. His response was to continue layoffs, strategically lie flat, and calculate P&L—working out the cost allocation for each product line and each small business, and for those that came out losing money, no one came to ask him for people anymore. He also gives an example: at the time the company had four IT staff, and even moving offices required hiring an outside contractor; now with one IT person, moving doesn't require an outside company either.

Technology that compresses modalities such as sound into token representations.

quotes.text: There's a saying: a Vision without a path and rhythm plan is hooliganism.
It was inevitably going to be like this, what's the big deal, its own big price cut, inevitably like this, and it will approach zero, infinitely close to zero.

Today you are in a sea where the situation is particularly unclear, and you are on a block of ice, what you're doing now is on a block of ice, but at least you are not underwater, you are on the ice, but this thing of yours may at any time—the ice will melt, or it will flip.
This may be the first time in the last two months that I've seen the sun set.

You find that entrepreneurs really sometimes—in the last month, having collected ten million, start thinking, oh, then on average I'll probably do twenty million a month, a year has twelve months, so my revenue for the next year will be two hundred and forty million.
Many companies, tech companies, enter a negative cycle from day one.
Does today's result do justice to my past efforts, does it do justice to the hardships I've endured over these 12 years? I think it does not.
